propositions.text: Whether union members formerly represented by their union have standing to maintain judicial review when the union no longer represents them but authorizes continuation.
propositions.quote: The principal issue raised on this consolidated application for judicial review is whether union members, formerly represented by their union at the grievance and adjudication phases, have standing to maintain an application for judicial review challenging a negative decision of an adjudicator in circumstances where the grievance relates to the interpretation of a provision of the collective agreement and their union no longer represents them, but purports to authorize the continuation of the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the main issue is whether former union members have standing for judicial review when the union no longer represents them but authorizes continuation.

propositions.text: The issue arises in the factual context described below.
propositions.quote: This issue arises in the following factual context.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the issue arises in the factual context that follows.

propositions.text: Applicants were employed by Canada Revenue Agency as large-file appeals officers at AU-04 level in Calgary and were members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada with a collective agreement.
propositions.quote: At all material times, the applicants were employed by the Canada Revenue Agency as large-file appeals officers at the AU-04 level in the Tax Services Office in Calgary, Alberta. The applicants were all members of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada and a collective agreement existed between the Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants were employed by Canada Revenue Agency as AU-04 appeals officers and were union members under a collective agreement.

propositions.text: Applicants filed grievances alleging employer violated clause 45.07 requiring acting pay for duties at higher classification for three days.
propositions.quote: The applicants, and others, filed grievances alleging that their employer had violated clause 45.07 of the collective agreement. This clause requires the payment of acting pay to an employee when the employee is required by the employer to substantially perform the duties of a higher classification level on an acting basis for three consecutive working days.

propositions.text: Applicants alleged they performed duties of AU-05 and AU-06 positions for a lengthy period.
propositions.quote: The applicants alleged that for a lengthy period they had been performing the duties associated with the positions classified at the AU-05 and AU-06 group and levels.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicants alleged employer violated acting pay clause and performed higher-level duties for a lengthy period.

propositions.text: Grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication under subsection 209(1) of FPSLR Act.
propositions.quote: The grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication pursuant to subsection 209(1) of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act, S.C. 2003, c. 22, s. 2 (FPSLR Act or Act).

propositions.text: Because grievance related to interpretation or application of collective agreement, applicants obtained Institute's approval to represent them in adjudication as required by subsection 209(2).
propositions.quote: Because the grievance related to “the interpretation or application in respect of the employee of a provision of a collective agreement”, the applicants obtained, as they were required to obtain, the approval of the Institute to represent them in the adjudication proceedings (subsection 209(2) of the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The court states grievances were consolidated and referred to adjudication with Institute's approval as required by law.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found she lacked jurisdiction because issues were classification, not acting pay.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator found that she was without jurisdiction to consider the grievances because the issues raised were issues of classification — not issues of acting pay.

propositions.text: If jurisdiction existed, Institute failed to show grievors assigned work outside AU-04 job description.
propositions.quote: The adjudicator went on to hold that if she was incorrect in that finding, the Institute had failed to meet the burden of showing that the grievors were assigned work outside the scope of the job description for their AU-04 large-file appeals officer positions (2017 PSLREB 45).

paragraphs.summary: The adjudicator found no jurisdiction as issues were classification, not acting pay, and Institute failed to prove grievors worked outside AU-04 scope.

propositions.text: Institute retained counsel to apply for judicial review; applicants later decided to represent themselves.
propositions.quote: The Institute retained counsel to commence an application for judicial review of the adjudicator’s decision, and counsel filed an application on behalf of each of the three applicants. After privileged discussions between the Institute and the applicants, it was decided that the applicants would represent themselves on the application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The adjudicator reports Institute retained counsel for judicial review but applicants chose to represent themselves.

propositions.text: Respondent Attorney General argues applicants lack standing to pursue application.
propositions.quote: In response, the respondent Attorney General argues that the applicants lack standing to pursue their application.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent Attorney General argues applicants lack standing to pursue the application.

propositions.text: Institute granted intervenor status on standing issue and filed affidavit authorizing continuation of application.
propositions.quote: The Institute was granted intervenor status in the application on the issue of whether the applicants have standing to pursue the application for judicial review in circumstances where they are no longer represented by the Institute’s counsel. The Institute’s General Counsel and Chief of Labour Relations Services has filed an affidavit in which she swears that the “Institute continues to authorize, support and approve the continuation” of the application.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute intervened on standing and filed affidavit authorizing continuation of the application.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review consolidated with others filed by applicants Fong and Leung after procedural removal.
propositions.quote: By order dated August 29, 2018, the application for judicial review was consolidated with other applications later filed by the applicants Mr. Fong and Mr. Leung after they were removed as parties from the original application for procedural reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court ordered consolidation of judicial review applications including those of Fong and Leung after procedural removal.

propositions.text: Issues are standing, adjudicator's jurisdiction, procedural fairness, bias, and reliance on perjured evidence.
propositions.quote: I would frame the issues raised by the applicants on this consolidated application to be: Do the applicants have standing to pursue the application for judicial review? Did the adjudicator commit a reviewable error in finding that she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate on the grievances? Did the adjudicator breach the applicants’ rights to procedural fairness or act in a manner that gives rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias? Did the adjudicator rely upon perjured evidence?

paragraphs.summary: The court frames issues as standing, jurisdiction, procedural fairness, bias, and perjured evidence reliance.

propositions.text: Attorney General argues applicants lack standing as not directly affected persons under Federal Courts Act.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the Attorney General argues that the applicants are not persons directly affected by the decision of the adjudicator as required by subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, because they seek a benefit under the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Applicants are not parties to collective agreement, which is exclusively between Institute and Canada Revenue Agency.
propositions.quote: However, they are not parties to this contract which is exclusively between the Institute and the Canada Revenue Agency.

propositions.text: Exclusivity principle means only union can pursue grievance.
propositions.quote: Counsel further argues that exclusivity between an employer and a union is a key principle in labour relations, and under this principle only the union can pursue a grievance.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues applicants lack standing as they are not parties to the collective agreement and only the union can pursue grievances.

propositions.text: Applicant Insch argues he has statutory and common law standing under FPSLR Act and Institute support.
propositions.quote: The applicant Ken Insch argues that he has both statutory and common law standing because the FPSLR Act contemplates judicial review in subsection 209(2), he signed the grievance and the Institute supports this application.

propositions.text: He is directly affected by adjudicator's denial of acting pay and by fraud, perjury, and egregious conduct before adjudicator.
propositions.quote: He further argues that he is directly affected by the adjudicator’s decision that denied him acting pay. Further, he argues he is directly affected by the fraud, perjury and egregious conduct that took place before the adjudicator and that the “government” owed him a duty of fairness.

propositions.text: Other applicants adopt these submissions.
propositions.quote: The other applicants adopt these submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant Insch argues he has standing, is directly affected by denial and misconduct, and others adopt these submissions.

propositions.text: Institute acknowledges it must support judicial review applications relating to collective agreement interpretation or administration.
propositions.quote: The Institute responds to the submissions of the Attorney General by acknowledging that the Institute must support any judicial review application relating to the interpretation or administration of the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Citing cases, Institute submits only union has carriage of disputes before Board concerning collective agreement interpretation and application.
propositions.quote: Citing cases such as Noël v. Société d'énergie de la Baie James, 2001 SCC 39, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 207 at paragraph 62 and Migneault v. New Brunswick (Board of Management), 2016 NBCA 52, 452 N.B.R. (2d) 223, the Institute submits that it is the union alone that has carriage of disputes before the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board (Board) that concern the interpretation and application of the governing collective agreement.

propositions.text: This ensures individual members cannot advance unsupported arguments about collective agreement interpretation or application.
propositions.quote: This requirement ensures that individual union members cannot advance an argument about the interpretation or application of a collective agreement that is not supported by the union as representative of all of the members of the relevant bargaining unit.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits only the union can carry disputes before the Board to ensure individual members do not advance unsupported arguments.

propositions.text: Under FPSLR Act, individual grievor files grievance and becomes applicant or respondent in judicial review.
propositions.quote: This said, the Institute submits that the grievance and adjudication scheme under the FPSLR Act and its predecessor is structured differently than in most other jurisdictions: under the Act it is the individual grievor who files the grievance in their name. Under this scheme it is the grievor who then becomes the applicant or respondent in an application for judicial review of a decision of an adjudicator.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits under FPSLR Act the individual grievor files grievance and becomes applicant or respondent in judicial review.

propositions.text: Institute must continue to support judicial review applications to maintain autonomy in policing collective agreement.
propositions.quote: The Institute submits, however, that it must continue to support any judicial review application relating to the interpretation or administration of the collective agreement, as it has in this case. Otherwise, its autonomy in policing the collective agreement would be undermined.

paragraphs.summary: The Institute submits it must continue to support judicial review applications to maintain its autonomy in policing the collective agreement.

propositions.text: Before considering issue, court refers to relevant provisions of collective agreement and FPSLR Act.
propositions.quote: Before beginning consideration of this issue it is helpful to first refer to the relevant provisions of the collective agreement and the FPSLR Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it will first refer to relevant provisions of the collective agreement and FPSLR Act before considering the issue.

propositions.text: The collective agreement is between Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.
propositions.quote: The collective agreement is between the Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the collective agreement is between Canada Revenue Agency and the Institute.

propositions.text: Article 25 recognizes Institute as exclusive bargaining agent for employees covered by certificate issued December 12, 2001.
propositions.quote: In article 25 of the collective agreement the employer recognized “the Institute as the exclusive bargaining agent for all employees described in the certificate issued by the Public Service Staff Relations Board on December 12, 2001, covering employees of the Audit, Financial and Scientific bargaining unit currently classified in accordance with” specified classification standards.

propositions.text: Applicants were employees described in this certificate.
propositions.quote: The applicants were employees described in this certificate.

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 25 recognizes Institute as exclusive bargaining agent for employees including applicants.

propositions.text: No provision grants individual employee unfettered right to pursue grievance if it relates to interpretation or application of collective agreement.
propositions.quote: No provision of the collective agreement grants to an individual employee the unfettered right to pursue a grievance at any level if the grievance relates to the interpretation or application of a provision of the collective agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no provision grants individual employees unfettered right to pursue grievances on collective agreement interpretation or application.

propositions.text: Article 34 of the agreement deals with the grievance procedure and limits individual grievances without union approval.
propositions.quote: article 34 of the agreement deals with the grievance procedure. An important limitation is found in article 34.07, which prevents an employee from presenting “an individual grievance relating to the interpretation or application … of a provision of a collective agreement … unless the employee has the approval of and is represented by the Institute.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 34 limits individual grievances without union approval under the grievance procedure.

propositions.text: Article 34.22 precludes individual grievance adjudication without union approval.
propositions.quote: article 34.22 precludes an employee from referring to adjudication an individual grievance relating to “the interpretation or application … of a provision of a collective agreement” without the approval of the Institute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states article 34.22 bars individual grievance adjudication without union approval.

propositions.text: Article 34 provisions largely reflect legislated requirements under the FPSLR Act.
propositions.quote: It will be seen from the following review of the relevant provisions of the FPSLR Act that the provisions of article 34 of the collective agreement in large measure reflect legislated requirements.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes article 34 largely reflects legislated requirements under the FPSLR Act.

propositions.text: The FPSLR Act preamble recognizes mutual respect and bargaining agents' role in workplace issues.
propositions.quote: The preamble to the Act recognizes that a “commitment from the employer and bargaining agents to mutual respect and harmonious labour-management relations is essential to a productive and effective public service”. The preamble also recognizes that “public service bargaining agents represent the interests of employees in collective bargaining and participate in the resolution of workplace issues and rights disputes”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the FPSLR Act preamble recognizes mutual respect and bargaining agents' role in workplace issues.

propositions.text: Subsection 2(1) defines collective agreement as a written agreement between employer and bargaining agent.
propositions.quote: Subsection 2(1) defines a “collective agreement” to be an agreement in writing “between the employer and a bargaining agent, containing provisions respecting terms and conditions of employment and related matters.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 2(1) defines collective agreement as a written agreement between employer and bargaining agent.

propositions.text: Part 1 defines parties as employer and bargaining agent; Part 2 has no parties definition.
propositions.quote: Part 1 of the Act, dealing with “Labour Relations”, defines “parties”, in relation to collective bargaining, arbitration, conciliation or a dispute, to mean “the employer and the bargaining agent.” (subsection 4(1)). Part 2 of the Act, dealing with “Grievances”, contains no definition of “parties”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Part 1 defines parties as employer and bargaining agent; Part 2 lacks a parties definition.

propositions.text: Subsection 208(1) entitles employees to present individual grievances with bargaining agent approval and representation.
propositions.quote: Subsection 208(1) of the Act states that “an employee is entitled to present an individual grievance” if the employee feels aggrieved “by the interpretation or application … of … a provision of a collective agreement”. The employee may only present the grievance if the employee “has the approval of and is represented by the bargaining agent for the bargaining unit to which the collective agreement” applies (subsection 208(4)).

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 208(1) entitles employees to present individual grievances with bargaining agent approval and representation.

propositions.text: Subsection 209(1) permits referral to adjudication with bargaining agent approval to represent the employee.
propositions.quote: Subsection 209(1) similarly permits an employee to refer to adjudication an individual grievance relating to “the interpretation or application … of a provision of a collective agreement”. Prior to referring the grievance, the employee must obtain “the approval of his or her bargaining agent to represent him or her in the adjudication proceedings.” (subsection 209(2)).

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 209(1) permits referral to adjudication with bargaining agent approval to represent the employee.

propositions.text: Regulations require grievor to have bargaining agent approval and representation for individual grievances.
propositions.quote: Section 67 of the Regulations permits an employee to present an individual grievance, while subsection 69(1) requires that a grievor who presents an individual grievance relating to the interpretation or application of a collective agreement must provide a declaration from the authorized representative of the appropriate bargaining agent indicating that the grievor, in presenting the grievance, has the approval of and is represented by the bargaining agent.

propositions.text: Notice of reference to adjudication must be filed in Form 20 with bargaining agent's declaration of representation willingness.
propositions.quote: Subsection 89(1) of the Regulations provides that a notice of reference to adjudication for individual grievances relating to the interpretation or application of a provision of the collective agreement shall be filed in Form 20 of the schedule. Form 20 collects information about the grievor and concludes with a declaration, in accordance with subsection 89(3), by an authorized representative of the applicable bargaining agent indicating that the bargaining agent is willing to represent the grievor in the adjudication proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states regulations require bargaining agent approval and Form 20 declaration for grievance adjudication references.

propositions.text: Adjudication rights arise from legislation, not the collective agreement, entitling employees to present grievances and refer to adjudication.
propositions.quote: The above review of the relevant provisions of the Act, Regulations and the collective agreement shows that adjudication rights in the federal public sector arise directly from the legislation and not the collective agreement: subject to the limitations described above, subsection 208(1) of the Act entitles an employee to present an individual grievance and subsection 209(1) entitles employees such as the applicants to refer individual grievances to adjudication.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds adjudication rights arise from legislation, not the collective agreement, entitling employees to present grievances and refer to adjudication.

propositions.text: Parties to adjudication are individual grievors and employer; union approves and represents but is not a party.
propositions.quote: Consistent with this legislation, the parties to an adjudication of an individual grievance before the Board are the individual grievors and the employer. The union is not a party but instead approves of and represents the employee at the grievance and adjudication stages.

propositions.text: Applicants do not exercise adjudication rights under the collective agreement between Institute and Canada Revenue Agency.
propositions.quote: Therefore, contrary to the submissions of the Attorney General, the applicants are not exercising adjudication rights under the collective agreement between the Institute and the Canada Revenue Agency.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties to adjudication are grievors and employer; union approves but is not party; applicants do not exercise rights under collective agreement.

propositions.text: Legislative scheme ousts contractual privity requirement relied on by Attorney General for adjudication rights.
propositions.quote: This legislative scheme, at least in respect of adjudication rights for individual grievances, ousts the requirement of contractual privity relied on by the Attorney General.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the legislative scheme ousts contractual privity requirement relied on by Attorney General for adjudication rights.

propositions.text: Federal Courts Act s.18.1(1) permits anyone directly affected to apply for judicial review.
propositions.quote: Subsection 18.1(1) of the Federal Courts Act permits anyone “directly affected by the matter in respect of which relief is sought” to apply for judicial review.

propositions.text: Attorney General argues applicants are not directly affected and lack standing to seek judicial review.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General has not demonstrated how as parties to an adjudication brought by the applicants under this statutory scheme, the applicants are not “directly affected” by the decision they seek to review.

propositions.text: Applicants have standing to commence and pursue judicial review as parties to adjudicator's decision.
propositions.quote: As parties to the adjudicator’s decision, the applicants have standing to commence and pursue this application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Federal Courts Act allows judicial review by those directly affected; Attorney General disputes applicants' standing; court finds applicants have standing.

propositions.text: Acknowledges difficulty posed by legislative scheme to union's role at judicial review stage.
propositions.quote: This said, I acknowledge the difficulty posed by this legislative scheme to the proper role of a union at the judicial review stage.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges difficulty posed by legislative scheme to union's role at judicial review stage.

propositions.text: Board and predecessors hold grievor may only proceed if represented by bargaining agent for grievances on collective agreement interpretation.
propositions.quote: The Board and its predecessors have consistently held that when a grievance relates to the interpretation or application of a collective agreement the grievor may only proceed if represented by his or her bargaining agent (see, for example, Cavanagh v. Canada Revenue Agency, 2014 PSLRB 21, [2014] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 21; Boivin v. Treasury Board (Canada Border Services Agency), 2009 PSLRB 98, [2009] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 98).

propositions.text: If bargaining agent withdraws support, grievance is no longer adjudicable.
propositions.quote: In such cases, if a bargaining agent subsequently withdraws its support, the grievance is no longer adjudicable (Yarney v. Deputy Head (Department of Health), 2011 PSLRB 112, [2011] C.P.S.L.R.B. No. 111).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker held grievors need bargaining agent representation for grievances; withdrawal ends adjudicability.

propositions.text: No similar statutory requirement exists for union representation at judicial review of adjudicator's negative decision.
propositions.quote: However, as the above review of the legislative regime and the collective agreement demonstrates, no similar statutory requirement exists when an employee pursues an application for judicial review of a negative decision of an adjudicator.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no statutory requirement for union representation at judicial review of adjudicator's negative decision.

propositions.text: Union representation protects all members' rights at grievance and adjudication stages for collective agreement interpretation.
propositions.quote: In a judicial review of a decision involving the interpretation or application of a provision of a collective agreement, the rights of all of a union’s members are at issue. At the grievance and adjudication stages the rights of all of the union’s members are protected by the requirement that the union represent grievors.

propositions.text: Union involvement ensures bargaining unit interests are protected during grievance and adjudication.
propositions.quote: This reflects the imperative that the union be involved in any grievance or adjudication that would interpret or apply the collective agreement so as to ensure that the interests of the bargaining unit as a whole are protected.

propositions.text: It makes little sense for union protection to be surrendered on judicial review, which has greater precedential value.
propositions.quote: In my view it makes little sense for the protection provided by union representation at the grievance and adjudication stages to be surrendered on judicial review — a proceeding that carries greater precedential value than grievance or adjudication proceedings.

propositions.text: Legislation provides no solution when union member pursues judicial review but union does not.
propositions.quote: However, the legislation provides no solution for the relatively rare situations when a union member wishes to pursue judicial review but the union does not.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds union representation protects members' rights at grievance and adjudication; no solution exists if union declines judicial review.

propositions.text: Institute submits union maintains ultimate control of grievance as it will represent grievors if matter remitted to adjudication.
propositions.quote: The Institute submits that in this circumstance the union maintains ultimate control of the grievance because if this Court remits the matter back to adjudication, the union will represent the grievors at adjudication.

propositions.text: Court notes this overlooks possibility of binding directions or outcome from this Court on adjudication.
propositions.quote: This, however, overlooks the potential for this Court to issue binding directions to an adjudicator or, in an exceptional case, to direct the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues union controls grievance if remitted; court finds this overlooks court's power to direct adjudication outcome.

propositions.text: Institute counsel drafted notice of application but applicants argue issues not raised by counsel, including inadequate representation and perjury allegations.
propositions.quote: Further, in the present case while counsel for the Institute did draft the notice of application seeking judicial review, in the consolidated application the applicants argue issues not raised by counsel in the application: that the applicants were inadequately represented by the Institute and that the employer, through specifically named employees, presented perjured evidence.

propositions.text: Serious unfiltered perjury allegation against co-workers may harm harmonious labour-management relations, a consequence of absent union representation on judicial review.
propositions.quote: Such a serious, unfiltered allegation of perjury made against co-workers cannot promote harmonious labour-management relations. Yet, it is a consequence that may flow from the absence of union representation on judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes applicants argue new issues including perjury allegations, which may harm labour relations without union representation on judicial review.

propositions.text: There may be a way to respect union's responsibility on judicial review when collective agreement interpretation issues arise.
propositions.quote: There is, perhaps, one way to recognize and respect on judicial review a union’s responsibility to ensure that the interests of the bargaining unit as a whole are protected when issues concerning the application or interpretation of a collective agreement are raised.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises the issue of a possible way to respect union responsibility on judicial review involving collective agreement interpretation.

propositions.text: Rule 303(1) requires naming as respondent every person directly affected by the order sought, except the tribunal itself
propositions.quote: Rule 303(1) of the Federal Courts Rules, in subpart (a), requires an applicant to name as a respondent every person “directly affected by the order sought in the application, other than a tribunal in respect of which the application is brought”

propositions.text: Applicants no longer represented by union may be required to name union as respondent and serve notice on union
propositions.quote: It may be that applicants who are no longer represented by their union on judicial review are required by this Rule to name the union as respondent in their notice of application and to serve their notice of application upon the union

propositions.text: Compliance with Rule 303(1) ensures affected union receives notice and can participate to protect bargaining unit interests
propositions.quote: Compliance with Rule 303(1) would ensure that an affected union receives notice of such an application and would permit the union to choose to participate in the proceeding to ensure that in matters that implicate the interpretation or application of the collective agreement the interests of the bargaining unit as a whole are represented and protected

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 303(1) requires naming all directly affected persons as respondents, possibly including unions, to protect bargaining unit interests.

propositions.text: Whether the adjudicator committed a reviewable error in finding she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate grievances
propositions.quote: Did the adjudicator commit a reviewable error in finding that she lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate on the grievances?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether the adjudicator erred in finding lack of jurisdiction over grievances.

propositions.text: Standard of review of correctness should apply to adjudicator's jurisdiction finding
propositions.quote: applicants’ submission that the standard of review of correctness should be applied to the adjudicator’s finding that she lacked jurisdiction to consider the grievances

propositions.text: Adjudicator's jurisdiction decision is reviewed for reasonableness, not correctness, citing Nadeau and Klos
propositions.quote: The adjudicator’s decision that she lacked jurisdiction is properly reviewed for reasonableness: Nadeau v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 203, [2018] F.C.J. No. 1133, paragraph 16; Klos v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 160, [2018] F.C.J. No. 916, paragraphs 1-3

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue correctness standard applies; court finds reasonableness standard applies to adjudicator's jurisdiction decision.

propositions.text: Adjudicator erred by misconstruing grievances as classification issues, constituting abuse of discretion and jurisdiction error
propositions.quote: applicants’ submission that by misconstruing the grievances to raise an issue of classification the adjudicator committed an error of law that rose to the level of an abuse of discretion and an error of jurisdiction

propositions.text: Applicants' submission of error in classification issue misconstruction has no merit
propositions.quote: There is equally no merit to the applicants’ submission that by misconstruing the grievances to raise an issue of classification the adjudicator committed an error of law that rose to the level of an abuse of discretion and an error of jurisdiction

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue adjudicator erred by misconstruing grievances; court finds no merit in this submission.

propositions.text: Applicants made few submissions addressing adjudicator's lack of jurisdiction finding and pointed to no clear errors
propositions.quote: The applicants made few if any submissions directly addressing the adjudicator’s finding that she lacked jurisdiction; the applicants do not point to any clear errors in the adjudicator’s reasoning

propositions.text: Applicants mainly argued case de novo and on fraudulent concealment, which Board did not determine due to lack of jurisdiction
propositions.quote: Rather, the bulk of the applicants’ submissions focus on arguing their case de novo and on the issue of fraudulent concealment, a matter not determined by the Board in view of its finding that it lacked jurisdiction

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicants did not clearly challenge adjudicator's jurisdiction finding but argued case anew and on fraudulent concealment.

propositions.text: Adjudicator referred to Bungay decision describing characteristics distinguishing classification from acting pay grievances
propositions.quote: the adjudicator referred to the decision of Bungay v. Treasury Board... where... the Board provided a non-exhaustive description of the characteristics that distinguish a classification grievance from an acting pay grievance

paragraphs.summary: The adjudicator relied on Bungay decision to distinguish classification grievances from acting pay grievances.

propositions.text: Adjudicator found applicants' concerns related to entire duties since appointment and consistent over time, suggesting chronic undervaluation
propositions.quote: The adjudicator found that the applicants’ concerns related to the entirety of their duties since their respective appointments to the AU-04 large-file appeals officer positions and that their duties had been consistent over time. This suggested that the applicants’ concern was that their work had been chronically undervalued

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found applicants' concerns involved entire duties consistently over time, indicating chronic undervaluation.

propositions.text: Applicants' grievances partly based on comparison with counterparts in another office
propositions.quote: The adjudicator further considered that the applicants’ grievances were in part based on a comparison with the work of their counterparts in another appeals office

propositions.text: Adjudicator found issues raised related to classification, a factually-suffused determination entitled to deference
propositions.quote: the adjudicator then looked at the essence of the applicants’ complaint and found that the issues they raised related to classification (reasons, paragraph 224). This was a heavily factually-suffused determination, based on the adjudicator’s appreciation of the evidence. It is a determination that is entitled to deference

propositions.text: Applicants have not shown the adjudicator's classification finding was unreasonable
propositions.quote: The applicants have not demonstrated that the finding was unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: Adjudicator found grievances related to classification; court finds this fact-based finding reasonable and entitled to deference.

propositions.text: Adjudicator breached procedural fairness by excluding some applicant evidence but allowing all employer evidence, causing bias
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that the adjudicator breached their right to procedural fairness by failing to admit some of their evidence, while allowing all of their employer’s evidence. This is said to have resulted in a biased procedure

propositions.text: Adjudicator showed reasonable apprehension of bias by relying almost exclusively on employer testimony despite equal applicant credibility
propositions.quote: The applicants further submit that the adjudicator demonstrated a reasonable apprehension of bias since she used the employer’s “representatives’ testimony almost exclusively as the basis for the Decision even though the Applicants were found to be equally credible”

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege procedural fairness breach and reasonable apprehension of bias due to exclusion of their evidence and reliance on employer testimony.

propositions.text: Applicants argue evidence was excluded as outside grievance period
propositions.quote: The applicants argue that their evidence was excluded on the basis that it was from “outside the grievance period”

propositions.text: No hearing transcript exists; court relies on affidavit evidence
propositions.quote: There is no transcript of the hearing before the adjudicator, which makes this Court reliant on affidavit evidence

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue evidence excluded as outside grievance period; court notes reliance on affidavit evidence due to no transcript.

propositions.text: Adjudicator excluded June 2, 2005 memorandum due to lack of testimony from sender/contact and irrelevance to applicants' division
propositions.quote: the affidavit of a representative of the employer is to the effect that neither the sender nor the contact person indicated on the document testified and the bargaining agent did not call any witness who had received the document. Further, the document only spoke about the Audit Division; the applicants were employed in the Appeals Division

propositions.text: These facts justify exclusion of the memorandum; employer's representative was not challenged in cross-examination
propositions.quote: These facts would justify exclusion of the memorandum and the employer’s representative was not challenged in cross-examination on her evidence

paragraphs.summary: Court finds exclusion of June 2, 2005 memorandum justified due to lack of testimony and irrelevance to applicants' division.

propositions.text: March 21, 2003 memorandum excluded because no witness connected it to applicant Mr. Fong and no sender/recipient testified
propositions.quote: the document was excluded because the bargaining agent could not connect it to the witness, the applicant Mr. Fong. Neither the sender nor the recipient of the memorandum or the purported author testified at the hearing

propositions.text: These facts justify exclusion of the memorandum
propositions.quote: These facts would also justify exclusion of this memorandum

paragraphs.summary: Court finds exclusion of March 21, 2003 memorandum justified due to lack of witness connection and testimony.

propositions.text: Similar examples of evidence exclusion exist
propositions.quote: Similar examples exist

paragraphs.summary: Court notes other similar examples of evidence exclusion.

propositions.text: Courts should not substitute their view of evidence relevance for decision-maker's except when exclusion breaches natural justice
propositions.quote: Courts generally should not substitute their view of the relevance of evidence for that of the decision-maker except when the rejection of relevant evidence has such an impact on the fairness of the proceeding that it unavoidably leads to the conclusion that there is been a breach of natural justice

paragraphs.summary: Court states courts should defer to decision-maker's evidence relevance unless exclusion breaches natural justice.

propositions.text: No basis found to conclude documents were improperly excluded causing breach of natural justice or bias
propositions.quote: In the absence of better evidence from the applicants I see no basis to find that documents were improperly excluded in a fashion that demonstrates any breach of natural justice or any reasonable apprehension of bias

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no evidence that document exclusion breached natural justice or caused bias.

propositions.text: Adjudicator's reliance on employer evidence does not support bias allegation
propositions.quote: Similarly, the adjudicator’s reliance upon evidence adduced by representatives of the employer cannot support the applicants’ allegation of bias

propositions.text: Bias is serious and requires evidence showing reasonable apprehension of unfairness
propositions.quote: Bias is a serious allegation. The applicants have not brought any evidence or argument that would demonstrate to a reasonable, fully informed person, thinking the matter through, that it is more likely than not that the adjudicator would not decide the matter before her fairly

propositions.text: Disagreement with adjudicator's evidence assessment does not amount to bias
propositions.quote: Mere disagreement with the way in which the adjudicator assessed conflicting evidence does not give rise to a valid claim of bias

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no bias as applicants provide no evidence; mere disagreement with evidence assessment is insufficient.

propositions.text: Applicants allege Canada Revenue Agency submitted perjured evidence
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that the Canada Revenue Agency, through its employees, submitted perjured evidence

propositions.text: Perjury is serious and requires more than mere assertion
propositions.quote: Perjury is also a serious allegation that must be supported by more than mere assertion

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege perjury by Canada Revenue Agency; court states perjury requires more than assertion.

propositions.text: Applicants argue every contradiction is continuation of fraud by management
propositions.quote: the applicants’ submissions are to the effect that since fraud has been perpetrated against them by their management team, every contradiction in the evidence is an apparent continuation of the fraud

propositions.text: Alleged lies are disagreements with evidence and requests to reweigh; applicants fail to demonstrate perjury
propositions.quote: the alleged lies or instances of perjury are best characterized as disagreements with the evidence adduced on behalf of the Canada Revenue Agency, and many of the applicants’ submissions on this issue amount to a request to reweigh the evidence that was before the adjudicator. The applicants have fallen well short of demonstrating perjury

paragraphs.summary: Applicants claim contradictions are fraud continuation; court finds these are disagreements and no perjury shown.

propositions.text: Dismiss application for judicial review; adjudicator's jurisdiction decision reasonable and not tainted by bias or impropriety
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the application for judicial review on the basis that the decision of the adjudicator that the Board lacked jurisdiction was reasonable, and the applicants have failed to demonstrate that this conclusion was tainted by bias or other impropriety

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application, finding adjudicator's jurisdiction decision reasonable and unbiased.

propositions.text: No order as to costs due to divided success on issues before the Court
propositions.quote: As success on the issues before the Court was divided I would not make any order as to costs

paragraphs.summary: Court declines to order costs due to divided success on issues.
